prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms confined at a magic wavelength are interrogated in parallel and reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep B052 as the sole prize part, and my preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: Katori and Ye, one part. The chair asked what separates the lattice clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes in physical terms, and I think there is a real answer. The comb prize honoured the ability to count optical cycles; the 2012 prize honoured control and spectroscopy of a single trapped ion. Neither contains the idea that a neutral-atom ensemble can be held in a lattice at a wavelength where the clock-transition light shift cancels, with Lamb-Dicke confinement removing Doppler and recoil, so that thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. That is a new mechanism, and it changes the statistical reach of the measurement by orders of magnitude, which is why the 1e-18 regime was reached in neutral atoms. It also made new physics observable: gravitational redshift across millimetre scales within a single sample, many-body effects in the clock, and sensitivity to ultralight dark matter and varying constants. A citation framed on the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and its realization, and not on optical clocks in general, would answer the increment objection. On timing, the confirmed performance has been reproduced by independent laboratories and species, and the redefinition of the second is a decision for other bodies that the physics does not depend on. On attribution, the two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, since Katori proposed the scheme and Ye drove it to the accuracy and many-body frontier. I would still describe the choice as a judgement among imperfect options and not as a clear win on conceptual breadth.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains overlap with the metrology lineage honoured in 2005 and 2012, and the fact that the real payoff, a redefined second and operational relativistic geodesy, has not yet arrived. A second concern is that Mehlig and Eriksson set conceptually broader candidates (B044, B021) above a precision advance, and I cannot dismiss that ordering on physics alone; I prefer B052 mainly because those candidates carry credit problems that a citation cannot repair. Third, groups at PTB, SYRTE, NIST and in Tokyo built much of the strontium and ytterbium ecosystem, and the two-name list leaves them out, so the citation wording must be precise about what Katori and Ye each did. Finally, my own priority recollections for the early magic-wavelength proposals are not verified in the supplied files.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B044 first with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, arguing for conceptual originality, a clean Jaksch-Zoller to Greiner-Bloch chain, and mature confirmation, and he accepts B052 as acceptable if attribution certainty is preferred to breadth.
responses.response: I take the B044 case more seriously after round 1 than I did in my opening, and I have moved it into my alternatives for that reason. The superfluid to Mott transition and the quantum gas microscope are a qualitative change in what can be measured, and the Jaksch-Zoller to Greiner-Bloch chain is as clean a theory-experiment story as the shortlist offers. My difficulty is the one you name yourself: Esslinger's fermionic work is central to the Hubbard programme, Zoller also sits on B009, and a three-name list forces an exclusion that I cannot justify on physics grounds. You also ask whether analogue simulation has yet delivered a decisive scientific result or is still a maturing platform; I do not think the files settle that, and I would rather not award a platform before it does. Since you say you are comfortable with B052 if the committee wants attribution certainty, I read our disagreement as one of weighting between novelty and credit risk, not of physics, and I would accept B044 as a sequenced later prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B021) first as a new class of matter, would narrow the citation to the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant, and would accept B052 if the attribution is judged irreparable.
responses.response: I agree that B021 is the conceptually richest candidate and I do not doubt its maturity. The narrowing you propose is the honest way to write it, but it does not solve the problem for me, because the experimental claim depends on the HgTe proposal. Without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang the citation would credit the observation of an effect without crediting the people who told the experimenters where to look, and Lindroth and Mehlig have said the same. The 2016 prize also leaves me uneasy about the apparent continuity of the story, although you are right that Z2 classification with time-reversal protection is a separate discovery from the integer quantum Hall and Haldane setting. Since you say you would accept B052 on attribution grounds, I take that as a convergence on the practical choice, not on the ranking of the physics.

responses.point: Olsson argues that aberration correction (B011) is the most original and least replaceable contribution and fits a measurement-enabling criterion as well as the clock, while conceding B052 is the strongest consensus candidate.
responses.response: I accept that Scherzer's limit was a real barrier and that its removal changed what can be seen in materials, so I do not treat B011 as lesser science. The reason I place the clock above it is the criterion of what is directly tested: the lattice clock provides measurements bearing on gravitational redshift, constants and dark matter, which are questions in fundamental physics, while aberration correction is a powerful instrument whose output is primarily structural information in materials. A second difficulty is the one you raise, that the TEM lineage of Rose, Haider and Urban and the STEM lineage of Krivanek and Dellby cannot both be credited in three names. For B052 the equivalent gap, other lattice-clock groups, is smaller because the scheme is credited to a proposer and a record-setting realiser. I also agree with you that a two-part prize combining B052 and B011 would break the three-person limit unless B011 were split, which I would not support.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved to B052 from the Higgs discovery (B010) because of its low attribution risk, while still regarding B010 as having greater scientific weight, and asks whether the Higgs discovery can fairly be assigned to three people.
responses.response: I share your assessment of the scientific weight of the Higgs discovery, and on that scale the clock is not comparable. My answer to your closing question is still no on the supplied credit: Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are founders and spokespersons who differ from the 2012 analysis leaders, so a citation would have to defend why founders rather than analysts, and that is fragile for a result obtained by thousands. I would not support B010 as a sole prize this year on that trio. I also note that you are chairing and that B052, your preferred part, carries no conflict flag on your side, while your closeness to B010 and B043 is disclosed. On the second question, I agree that the chair's two-part option does not help, since any second part would push the configuration past three people.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B052 as a measurement-limited advance, discloses a doctoral research stay in the JILA environment of Hall, and asks whether disclosure or recusal is needed.
responses.response: I agree with your account of the mechanism and I have used it in my answer to the chair's first question, with one difference of emphasis: I would not describe the value of the clock as the measurement-limited number but as the capability it opens for tests of relativity and constants, so the citation should name that. On your disclosure, a research stay in the laboratory where Ye trained, without co-authorship, seems to me a matter for the chair to record and not a reason for recusal, but I note that the question is the chair's, and I would be more comfortable if the committee minuted it before the vote. I also share your concern, which I put in my uncertainties, that enthusiasm for precision measurements may be a shared bias among the members preferring B052.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the magic-wavelength lattice scheme as a distinct discovery from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on how the citation is worded.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would strengthen or merely delay the case; I hold that the physics does not require it.

Early priority among the magic-wavelength proposals and the first strontium demonstrations is recalled from memory and is not verified in the supplied files, so a third name from the PTB, SYRTE, NIST or Tokyo groups cannot be excluded by me on evidence.
Whether the conceptually broader candidates B044 and B021 deserve to outrank a precision advance if their attribution problems were resolved; I cannot settle this from the supplied credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group), none of which link to Katori, Ye or the shortlisted alternatives. My field is high-energy theory and cosmology, which is why I lean on colleagues for the atomic-physics details of B052, B044 and B056. No recusal is needed on my side.
